1958 Chevrolet Bel Air Gets First Cleaning in Decades, Morphs Into Stunning Survivor
14 photos
Photo: Theetravisb/YouTube
In 1958, General Motors celebrated 50 years in business with anniversary models for all divisions. For Chevrolet, this meant the introduction of new nameplates, including the iconic Impala , Biscayne, Yeoman, and Brookwood.
That same year also saw the discontinuation of the 150 and 210 models. However, Chevrolet kept both the Bel Air and Nomad in production. The latter retained its top position in the station wagon lineup, while the Bel Air slotted between the Biscayne and the Impala.
While the brand-new Impala was restricted to two-door body styles, the Bel Air was also available as a four-door sedan and hardtop. Much like its fancier sibling, the 1958 Bel Air is a one-year-old design. In 1959, Chevrolet gave its full-size car lineup a complete overhaul.
Several decades later, the Impala is arguably the most desirable Chevy of the 1958 bunch. The Bel Air doesn't get as much attention, and very few actually care about the four-door version. However, this sedan definitely deserves some time in the spotlight. It's one of those cool unrestored survivors.
Showcased by YouTube's "Theetravisb," this Bel Air spent most of its life with its original owner. The vehicle was retired in a backyard some decades ago and remained there even after the original owner passed away in 2012. More recently, however, it was auctioned off along with other things from the said estate, and found a new owner.
Fortunately, our host did not purchase the Chevrolet for parts or to flip after a bit of maintenance. He gave it a proper scrubbing, turning it into a stunning time capsule.
What sets this Bel Air apart from all the other undesirable Chevys? Well, for starters, it took decades of storage like a champ. This sedan is essentially rust-free, which is downright surprising given that it sat under full exposure to the elements for a while. Moreover, it's amazingly original .
It still rocks the original paint, which still looks good after proper cleaning and buffing. By the way, this Colonial Cream and Arctic White color combo isn't very common either. The interior looks even better, with the turquoise/teal upholstery showing next to no wear and tear (for a vehicle that's a whopping 68 years old).
The original engine is still under the hood, albeit it's not the desirable 348-cubic-inch (5.7-liter) W-series big-block V8. But it's not the entry-level 235-cubic-inch (3.9-liter) Blue Flame inline-six either. This Bel Air was fitted with the optional 283-cubic-inch (4.6-liter) small-block V8. It mates with an automatic transmission.
Although it may not be the most desirable Bel Air out there, this Chevy is a spectacular find. You just don't see unrestored survivors like this very often. Like our host puts it, this car should be in a museum. But I also think it deserves some time on the road. Check it out in the video below.
